What an Advisor Does for a Web3 Company

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 25 February 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Strategy

A useful Web3 advisor helps founders make a small number of consequential, often irreversible decisions well: which audience moves first, how much to spend on incentives, which decisions need counsel, where distribution exists beyond the crypto timeline, what institutions need, and when to say "you are not ready". The structure matters as much as the advice. US and EU rules treat undisclosed paid promotion and public promises as legal facts, so put the scope in writing, lock the tokens and disclose every connection.

This is not legal advice. Advisor arrangements and token allocations are fact-specific; get your own counsel.

For a few years, "advisor" in Web3 meant a wallet address on a token allocation and a headshot on a website. The advisor posted on launch day and was never heard from again. The category earned its reputation.

That model is gone, and what replaces it looks more like advisory in any other industry: experienced people helping founders make a small number of consequential decisions well. Our guide to agency vs consultancy vs advisor sets out where advisory sits among the alternatives. The decisions in Web3 are unusual enough that the help is worth having.

What is different about Web3 decisions

Many of them are irreversible in a literal sense. A token, once distributed, cannot be recalled. A contract, once live on-chain, is public and permanent. A treasury action is on-chain for good. A regulatory posture, once a product is live in a jurisdiction, has been observed.

The record of what happens when those decisions go wrong is public. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with one exchange compromise accounting for $1.5 billion. Academic analysis of nine major airdrops found up to 66% of claimed tokens went to exchanges in the first transfer, a distribution decision that cannot be reversed once made.

And the company usually faces several audiences at once: users, developers, liquidity providers, partners, institutions and community, each of which has to believe something different before the system works. Sequencing those audiences is the central go-to-market problem, and most founders are solving it for the first time. Our playbook on the multi-audience launch plan covers the sequence itself.

What a useful advisor contributes

ContributionWhat it looks like in practiceThe question the advisor keeps asking
SequencingNaming which audience must move first and what evidence it needs; holding announcements that are earlyWhich of the markets around this product is the real constraint?
Restraint on incentivesReviewing points, airdrops and ambassador programmes before they are announcedWhat behaviour is rewarded, how is it farmed, and what remains when it stops?
Regulatory postureJudgment about which decisions need counsel first, which jurisdictions to launch in and what not to sayHas a lawyer seen this before we commit to it in public?
Distribution beyond the timelinePointing to affiliate, partner, disclosed creator programmes, owned email and programmaticWho already holds the customer we want?
Institutional translationExplaining what diligence requires, who needs to be in the room and how long it takesWhat will the allocator's risk team ask in week three?
A credible noSaying "you are not ready to launch this" when the community wants the announcementWhat happens to the company if this goes wrong next week?

Sequencing. An advisor who has watched several launches can see the dependency chain the team is too close to notice, and can say which audience is actually the constraint.

Restraint on incentives. Points, airdrops and ambassador programmes are the most effective and most misused tools in the category. Our analysis of airdrops and points sets out the evidence: Nansen found 41.1% of the top 10,000 ZKsync recipients sold their entire allocation within a day. The useful advisor asks the hard questions before the programme is announced rather than after.

Regulatory posture. Not legal advice, but judgment. The 2026 position makes that judgment more specific. In the US, the SEC and CFTC interpretation of 17 March 2026 sorts tokens into categories and says a token can be tied to an investment contract through the issuer's promises, weighing who made them, when and through which medium. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets of August 2026 is still a proposal, and the CLARITY Act failed Senate cloture 49 to 50 in September 2026. In the EU, MiCA requires marketing to be consistent with the white paper, and its transitional period for service providers ended on 1 July 2026. The cheapest advice in Web3 is "ask a lawyer first", and it is rarely taken without someone in the room insisting on it.

Distribution beyond the timeline. Crypto-native distribution runs through a small set of channels: the timeline, a handful of communities, KOLs and exchange listings. Those channels are crowded and expensive. An advisor with experience outside the category can point to the open channels the crypto-native playbook ignores, which our piece on distribution when ad platforms restrict you describes, and to ecosystem-led growth through partners who already hold the customer.

Institutional translation. For projects selling to funds, custodians, banks or enterprises, an advisor who has sat on the buying side can explain what diligence requires, who needs to be in the room and how long it takes. That is the difference between a pipeline and a list of logos.

A credible no. The most valuable sentence an advisor says is "you are not ready to launch this." Founders surrounded by a community and a timeline that want the announcement need one person whose incentive is the company's survival rather than the week's excitement.

The most valuable sentence an advisor says is "you are not ready to launch this."

How to structure it

The same rules as anywhere else, applied more strictly, because the regulators have already shown what goes wrong.

TermWhat good looks likeWhy it matters in 2026
Written scopeNamed decisions the advisor helps with, and a named founder who prepares each sessionMakes the advice auditable and the relationship easy to end
VestingA cliff on tokens as well as equity, with a lock that survives the token launchThe SEC's 2026 proposal treats lockups and release schedules as part of token-economics disclosure
ConflictsDisclosure of every other project the advisor touches, checked for conflictsCompeting allocations distort the advice on sequencing and incentives
Public promotionNone, unless disclosed and agreed in writingThe FTC requires material connections to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously; the SEC's 2022 case over an undisclosed $250,000 post ended in a $1.26 million settlement
Public statementsAdvisors do not make promises about the token, price or roadmapUnder the 2026 interpretation, public promises of managerial effort feed the securities analysis

The decisions themselves deserve a record: what was decided, why, who owned it and what was expected. A short decision record per session makes an advisor's contribution visible, and makes it obvious when there was none. Our build order for crypto and digital assets shows where that record belongs in the commercial system.

The signal of a good one

They ask about the customer before the token. They ask what the product does for someone who does not care about crypto. They ask what happens when the incentives stop. They ask who has reviewed the claims on the website. And they are willing to be the least popular person in the launch channel for a week.

The same tests apply to advisors for AI companies, which our piece on what advisors do for AI companies covers. The Web3 version simply has less room for error.

lowob takeaways

  • Few decisions, high stakes. Distributed tokens, live contracts and on-chain treasury actions cannot be undone.
  • Six contributions. Sequencing, restraint, regulatory judgment, distribution beyond the timeline, institutional translation and a credible no.
  • Regulatory posture is judgment, not legal advice. The advisor's job is to get counsel into the room before the commitment.
  • Structure it in writing. Scope, vesting with a lock past launch, disclosed conflicts and no undisclosed promotion.

Common questions

What does a Web3 advisor actually do?

Helps founders sequence which audience moves first, restrains incentive programmes, judges which decisions need counsel, finds distribution beyond crypto-native channels, translates for institutions and says when the team is not ready to launch.

How should a Web3 advisor agreement be structured?

A written scope, vesting with a cliff on tokens and equity, a lock that survives the token launch, disclosure of other projects checked for conflicts, and no public promotion unless disclosed and agreed in writing.

Can a crypto advisor promote the token they are paid in?

Only with clear disclosure, and ideally not at all. The FTC requires material connections in endorsements to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, and the SEC has fined promoters who did not disclose compensation for touting a crypto asset security.

How do I spot a good crypto advisor?

They ask about the customer before the token, what the product does for someone who does not care about crypto, what happens when incentives stop, and who reviewed the public claims.

Next move

Before announcing the next incentive programme, ask what behaviour it rewards, how it can be farmed and what remains when it stops. If you have advisors, check that each agreement has a written scope, a token lock that survives launch and a disclosure clause.
